title: Agglutinative Morphology and Predicative Suffixes
subtitle: Forming plural nouns and identifying who you are without using 'to be'
keyPoint: Uzbek chains suffixes together systematically: plural -lar attaches directly to the stem, followed by person endings like -man or -miz.

mistakes.note: The plural marker -lar must come before the predicative person ending -miz.
The suffix -man is exclusively for the first person (I); third person does not take -man.
Match the 3rd person plural subject 'ular' with the plural suffix -lar instead of first person.

quiz.question: Complete the sentence: 'Men o'qituvchi___.' (I am a teacher)
quiz.explanation: The first-person singular predicative suffix in Uzbek is '-man'.

quiz.question: How do you say 'We are doctors' in Uzbek?
quiz.explanation: For 'we', use the first-person plural ending '-miz'.

quiz.question: Choose the correctly stacked form for 'We are students':
quiz.explanation: The plural marker '-lar' precedes the person ending '-miz'.

quiz.question: Complete the sentence: 'Sen juda mehribon___.' (You are very kind)
quiz.explanation: The second-person singular informal ending is '-san'.

tip: Uzbek has no present-tense copula verb like 'is' or 'am'; simply glue the appropriate personal ending directly onto the noun or adjective!

title: The Six Noun Cases
subtitle: Navigating direction, location, origin, and objects with case endings
keyPoint: Case endings attach to the end of nouns to define their role, such as movement toward (-ga), location at (-da), or origin from (-dan).

mistakes.note: Direction towards a place requires the dative case ending -ga.
Being located inside or at a place requires the locative case suffix -da.
Use the unmarked nominative for general/indefinite objects; use -ni only for specific, definite objects.

quiz.question: Which suffix indicates movement toward a place? ('to')
quiz.explanation: The dative suffix '-ga' denotes movement toward a goal or destination.

quiz.question: Complete the sentence: 'Ular Samarqand___ poyezdda kelishdi.' (from Samarkand)
quiz.explanation: The ablative suffix '-dan' means 'from'.

quiz.question: Choose the correct locative form for 'in the classroom' (sinf):
quiz.explanation: The locative suffix '-da' indicates location within or at a place.

quiz.question: Which case marker marks a definite direct object ('the book')?
quiz.explanation: The accusative suffix '-ni' marks specific and definite direct objects.

tip: Remember that -ga becomes -ka after words ending in 'k' (masalan: bog'cha -> bog'chaga, but erkak -> erkakka) and -qa after 'q' (qishloq -> qishloqqa).

title: Possessive Suffixes and Izafet Constructions
subtitle: Expressing ownership and linking compound nouns
keyPoint: Possession is expressed by attaching personal possessive suffixes (-im, -ing, -i) to the possessed noun, matching the owner.

useCases.label: Noun Compounds (Izafet)
useCases.example: Toshkent shahri juda qadimiy va go'zal.

mistakes.note: Even if the possessive pronoun 'mening' is stated, the noun must still carry the possessive suffix -im.
Third-person possession on vowel-ending nouns requires -si.
The suffix must agree with 'bizning' (our), requiring -imiz, not third person -i.

quiz.question: Complete the phrase: 'Mening ruchka___' (My pen)
quiz.explanation: Since 'ruchka' ends with a vowel, the first-person singular possessive suffix is '-m'.

quiz.question: How do you say 'His/Her house' (uy)?
quiz.explanation: 'Uy' ends in a consonant, so the 3rd person singular ending is '-i'.

quiz.question: Complete: 'Bizning oila___ juda ahil.' (Our family)
quiz.explanation: For words ending in a vowel with 'bizning', use '-miz' (oilamiz).

quiz.question: Which compound correctly forms 'Chilonzor district' (tuman)?
quiz.explanation: Indefinite noun compounds attach the 3rd person suffix (-i/-si) to the second noun: Chilonzor tumani.

tip: When a noun ends in -q or -k and receives a vowel-initial possessive suffix, the consonant softens: yurak -> yuragim, quloq -> qulog'im.

title: Present-Future Tense (-a/-y)
subtitle: Talking about daily habits, routines, and scheduled future actions
keyPoint: Form this tense by adding -a (after consonants) or -y (after vowels) to the verb stem, followed by predicative personal endings.

useCases.label: Habitual Routines
useCases.example: Men har kuni soat yettida uyg'onaman.

examples.en: U har kuni ertalab choy ichadi.

mistakes.wrong: Men har kuni dars ishlayman (from ishla-).
mistakes.note: Always attach -y- to vowel-ending verb stems like ishla- -> ishlayman, never -a-.

mistakes.wrong: U non yemaydi -> U non yemaydi.
mistakes.note: Remember negative forms insert -ma- before -y-: ye + ma + y + di = yemaydi.
Person ending must agree with subject 'Biz': use -miz instead of singular -man.

quiz.question: How do you conjugate 'ishla-' (to work) for 'Men' (I)?
quiz.explanation: Since the stem 'ishla-' ends in a vowel, take '-y-' followed by '-man': ishlayman.

quiz.question: Complete the routine: 'U har kuni sport bilan shug'ullan___.' (He exercises every day)
quiz.explanation: 3rd person singular takes -a- + -di: shug'ullanadi.

quiz.question: What is the negative form of 'Men boraman' (I will go)?
quiz.explanation: Add negative suffix -ma- directly to the root: bor + ma + y + man = bormayman.

quiz.question: Complete the question: 'Siz choy ich___?' (Do you drink tea?)
quiz.explanation: For formal 'Siz', add stem + -a- + -siz + question particle -mi: ichasizmi?

tip: The present-future tense works like both the English simple present ('I work') and simple future ('I will work'). Context makes the timeframe clear!

title: Definite Past Tense (-di)
subtitle: Reporting witnessed, completed events with precision
keyPoint: The definite past tense attaches -di directly to the verb stem, using short personal endings (-m, -ng, —, -k, -ngiz, -lar).

examples.en: Ular Toshkentga erta tongda yetib kelishdi.

mistakes.note: The first-person plural ending for the -di past tense is -k (keldik), not -miz or -lar.
The definite past tense uses short endings (-m), not the copular ending (-man).
Negate past tense verbs using the suffix -ma- on the stem, never the word 'emas'.

quiz.question: Complete the sentence: 'Men kecha yangi uyga ko'ch___.' (I moved yesterday)
quiz.explanation: The 1st person singular ending in the definite past tense is '-dim'.

quiz.question: How do you say 'We saw' (ko'r-) in the definite past?
quiz.explanation: Past tense for 'we' takes the consonant ending '-k': ko'rdik.

quiz.question: Choose the correct negative form for 'She did not write':
quiz.explanation: Root yoz- + negative -ma- + past -di = yozmadi.

quiz.question: Complete the question: 'Siz bu filmni ko'r___?' (Did you watch this film?)
quiz.explanation: For polite/formal 'Siz', use '-dingiz' followed by the question particle '-mi': ko'rdingizmi?

tip: Notice that the past tense personal endings (-m, -ng, -k, -ngiz) resemble possessive endings rather than the predicative endings (-man, -san, -miz) used in the present!

title: Existential Predicates: Bor, Yoʻq, and Emas
subtitle: Expressing existence, possession, and nominal negation
keyPoint: Use 'bor' and 'yoʻq' for existence and possession ('there is / have' vs 'there is not / don't have'), but use 'emas' to negate equivalence or descriptions ('is not').

cells: There is a book / I have a book.
There is no book / I have no book.

mistakes.note: Use 'emas' to negate identity or occupation; 'yoʻq' means 'is absent' or 'does not exist'.
Possession requires 'bor' or 'yoʻq' alongside the locative case suffix '-da'.
Adjectives are negated using 'emas', never 'yoʻq'.

quiz.question: Choose the word to say 'I have no money': 'Menda pul ___.'
quiz.explanation: 'Yoʻq' expresses the absence of an item or possession.

quiz.question: Choose the word to say 'This car is not expensive': 'Bu mashina qimmat ___.'
quiz.explanation: Adjectival negation requires 'emas'.

quiz.question: Choose the word to ask 'Is there tea?': 'Choy ___?'
quiz.explanation: Add the question particle '-mi' to 'bor' to ask about existence.

quiz.question: Choose the word to say 'Farhod is not at home': 'Farhod uyda ___.'
quiz.explanation: 'Yoʻq' indicates physical absence from a location.

tip: Remember: 'emas' negates adjectives and noun identities ('is not'), while 'yoʻq' negates presence and possession ('there is not / does not have').

title: Present Continuous Aspect (-yotir, -moqda, -yap)
subtitle: Distinguishing colloquial vs. formal continuous actions
keyPoint: Use '-yap' in everyday spoken Uzbek and '-moqda' in formal speech, news broadcasts, and written literature to express ongoing actions.

mistakes.note: The infinitive suffix '-moq' must not be confused with continuous '-moqda' or spoken '-yap-'.
Do not insert an extra vowel; after consonant stems ending without clusters, attach '-yap-' directly (yoz + yap + ti).
Formal journalism strictly prefers '-moqda' over the conversational '-yap-' suffix.

quiz.question: Which verb form best fits official news: 'Universitet yangi bino ___'?
quiz.explanation: Formal written and media reports use '-moqda'.

quiz.question: How do you casually tell a friend 'I am listening to music': 'Men musiqa ___'?
quiz.explanation: Conversational speech typically uses the spoken progressive marker '-yap-' with person endings.

quiz.question: What is the third-person formal continuous form of 'ishlamoq' (to work)?
quiz.explanation: The suffix '-moqda' without personal endings indicates third-person formal continuous.

quiz.question: Choose the correct conversational form for 'Where are you going?': 'Qayerga ___?'
quiz.explanation: 'Boryapsiz' is the natural second-person polite continuous form in daily conversation.

tip: Use '-yap-' in 95% of daily interactions with friends and coworkers, but switch to '-moqda' when writing essays, official letters, or resumes.

title: Indefinite Past and Perfect (-gan)
subtitle: Talking about life experiences, unseen past, and completed states
keyPoint: Attach '-gan' plus personal endings to denote life experiences ('have done'), non-witnessed actions, or resulting past states.

mistakes.note: Use '-gan' for general experiential background ('have been to'), whereas '-di' denotes a specific direct past event.
Negate verbs in '-gan' using the verbal negative marker '-ma-' before the suffix, not 'emas'.
To form a question with '-gan', append the question particle '-mi' followed by personal predicate suffixes.

quiz.question: How do you say 'I have never read this book'?: 'Men bu kitobni hech qachon ___.'
quiz.explanation: Indefinite past experience with 'hech qachon' takes '-maganman'.

quiz.question: Which form asks 'Have you (polite) eaten plov before?'
quiz.explanation: 'Yeganmisiz' combines the experience suffix '-gan' with question marker '-mi' and polite suffix '-siz'.

quiz.question: What is the third-person form for 'He has arrived'?: 'U ___.'
quiz.explanation: The third-person singular needs no additional person suffix: just 'kelgan'.

quiz.question: Complete the sentence 'We have worked in this company': 'Biz bu korxonada ___.'
quiz.explanation: 'Biz' takes the first-person plural ending '-miz'.

tip: Think of '-gan' as English 'have done' (present perfect) — perfect for resumes and describing places you've visited or things you've tried.

title: Imperative and Voluntative-Optative Moods
subtitle: Commands, polite requests, and inclusive 'let's' proposals
keyPoint: Use the bare stem for informal commands, '-ing' for polite requests, and '-aylik' for collective suggestions ('let's').

examples.en: Bu yerda kutgin, men hozir qaytaman.

mistakes.note: Pairing 'iltimos' (please) with the informal bare stem is contradictory; use polite '-ing'.
To propose 'let's do something', use the voluntative suffix '-(a)ylik'.
Third person commands ('let him/her') take '-sin', not the second person '-ing'.

quiz.question: How do you politely invite someone to sit down?: 'Iltimos, ___.'
quiz.explanation: Polite requests directed at 'Siz' end with '-ing' / '-ingiz'.

quiz.question: Choose the correct form for 'Let's begin': 'Darsni ___.'
quiz.explanation: The optative suffix '-(a)ylik' means 'let us'.

quiz.question: How do you tell a friend casually 'Listen to me!'?: 'Meni ___!'
quiz.explanation: Informal direct commands to peers use the bare verb stem (or '-gin').

quiz.question: Choose the 3rd person command for 'Let Ahmad come': 'Ahmad ___.'
quiz.explanation: Third-person commands use the suffix '-sin'.

tip: Whenever you enter an Uzbek home or taxi, you will hear '-ing' forms like 'Kiring' (Come in) and 'Oʻtiring' (Sit down) — using '-ing' ensures you remain courteous.

title: Spatial Relational Nouns and Case Postpositions
subtitle: Navigating space and relations with spatial roots and case-governing words
keyPoint: Uzbek uses relational spatial nouns (ust-, tag-, ich-, old-) with possessive and case endings, alongside primary postpositions (bilan, uchun, keyin).

mistakes.note: Do not put locative '-da' on both nouns; attach it to the spatial noun ('stol ustida' or 'stolning ustida').
'Keyin' (after) governs the ablative case suffix '-dan' on the preceding noun.
While 'uchun' takes nominative nouns, ensure the noun itself reflects the intended number and possession accurately.

quiz.question: Choose the correct postposition: 'Men metro ___ ishga boraman.'
quiz.explanation: 'Bilan' means 'by / with' indicating means of transportation.

quiz.question: How do you say 'The cat is under the chair'?: 'Mushuk stulning ___.'
quiz.explanation: 'Tagida' translates to 'under / beneath' (tag + i + da).

quiz.question: Which case suffix must precede 'keyin' (after)?: 'Tushlik___ keyin uchrashamiz.'
quiz.explanation: 'Keyin' requires the preceding noun to take the ablative case ending '-dan'.

quiz.question: Fill the blank for 'inside the box': 'Quti ___ nima bor?'
quiz.explanation: 'Ichida' means 'inside' (ich + i + da).

tip: Construct spatial positions like a sandwich: [Noun] + [Spatial word] + [Possessive -i] + [Case -da/-ga/-dan] (e.g., uy + old + i + da = uy oldida 'in front of the house').

title: Comparison with Ablative Case and Eng
subtitle: Form comparative and superlative sentences in Uzbek
keyPoint: Attach the ablative suffix -dan to the point of comparison to express 'than', and place 'eng' directly before adjectives to make superlatives.

useCases.label: Absolute Superlative
useCases.example: Bu kutubxona shahardagi eng qadimgi bino.

mistakes.note: Use the ablative case suffix -dan directly on the pronoun or noun, not standalone English-like particles.
Do not combine the superlative marker 'eng' with the comparative suffix '-roq'.
The standard of comparison requires the ablative suffix -dan ('than his brother').

quiz.question: Toshkent Samarqand___ kattaroq.
quiz.explanation: The ablative case ending -dan marks the standard of comparison ('than Samarqand').

quiz.question: Bu dunyodagi ___ chiroyli shahar.
quiz.explanation: The word 'eng' precedes the adjective to form the superlative degree ('the most beautiful').

quiz.question: Mening ukam sen___ chaqqon.
quiz.explanation: Comparing two persons requires the ablative suffix -dan on the second person ('faster than you').

quiz.question: Bugun kechagidan ___ sovuq.
quiz.explanation: 'Ancha' functions as an intensifier meaning 'much/considerably colder than yesterday'.

tip: Use -roq alone when subtly shading an adjective (e.g. 'yaxshiroq' = 'better / rather good'), but rely on -dan when the comparison target is explicitly stated.

title: Basic Coordinating Converbs (-ib and -(a)rli)
subtitle: Chain actions smoothly using the coordinating converb -ib
keyPoint: Use the converb -ib (or -b after vowels) to link sequential actions sharing the same subject, leaving tense and personal markers for the final verb.

examples.en: Biz bozorga borib meva sotib oldik.

mistakes.note: While 'va' is grammatically possible, natural Uzbek prefers the converb -ib to link sequential verb clauses.
Converb -ib attaches directly to the bare verb stem (oʻqi- + -b), not to past tense conjugations.
The suffix -ib cannot stand alone without either a finite auxiliary or standard past endings unless intended as an inferential past.

quiz.question: Talaba darsni tingla___ daftarga yozdi.
quiz.explanation: The stem 'tingla-' ends in a vowel, so it takes the coordinating converb ending -b.

quiz.question: Ular choy ___ suhbatlashdilar.
quiz.explanation: 'Ichib' connects the prior action of drinking tea with the conversation verb.

quiz.question: Eshikni taqillat___ ichkariga kirdi.
quiz.explanation: 'Taqillat-' ends in a consonant and requires -ib to denote the preceding action.

quiz.question: Bolalar darsdan keyin uyga ___ vazifalarini bajardilar.
quiz.explanation: 'Qaytib' acts as the chained converb connecting returning home with doing homework.

tip: Only the final verb in a chain takes personal suffixes (e.g. -man, -san, -di). All preceding verbs take only -ib/-b, dramatically streamlining your sentences!

title: Compound Descriptive Verbs (-ib / -a + Auxiliary)
subtitle: Add nuanced shades of meaning using verbal compounds
keyPoint: Combine a lexical verb ending in -ib or -a/-y with auxiliary verbs like bermoq, koʻrmoq, and olmoq to express benefaction, experimentation, or ability.

examples.en: U menga yangi qoidani tushuntirib berdi.
Biz bu masalani hal qilib beramiz.

mistakes.note: The auxiliary verb 'olmoq' expressing ability requires the -a/-y converb, not -ib.

mistakes.right: Menga yordam berib yubor / yordam ber.
mistakes.note: 'Koʻrmoq' means to test or try out; for doing a favor for someone, use 'bermoq'.
Auxiliary structures must combine with a converb (-ib), never the infinitive (-moq).

quiz.question: Men bu ogʻir yukni koʻtara ___ .
quiz.explanation: The -a converb on 'koʻtara' pairs with 'olmoq' to express ability ('was able to lift').

quiz.question: Iltimos, menga xatni tarjima qilib ___ .
quiz.explanation: 'Qilib bermoq' conveys a polite request to do a favor for the speaker.

quiz.question: Bozorga borib yangi anorlardan tatib ___ .
quiz.explanation: 'Tatib koʻrmoq' means to try tasting something to test it.

quiz.question: U kutilmagan xabardan yigʻlab ___ .
quiz.explanation: '-ib yubormoq' marks a sudden, involuntary burst of emotion or action.

tip: Pay close attention to the converb vowel: '-a olmoq' signifies possibility and capability, whereas '-ib olmoq' means to do something for one's own benefit!

title: Participles as Relative Clauses (-gan, -digan, -adigan)
subtitle: Form modifier clauses without relative pronouns using participles
keyPoint: Uzbek has no relative pronouns like 'who' or 'which'; instead, relative clauses precede nouns using participle suffixes (-gan for past/completed, -(a)digan for habitual/present).

cells: the person who works / will work

useCases.label: Past Completed Relative Clause
useCases.example: Biz kecha koʻrgan film juda qiziq edi.

useCases.label: Action in Progress
useCases.example: Hozir nutq soʻzlayotgan kishi bizning dekanimiz.

examples.en: Men sotib olgan kitob juda qimmat ekan.
Kutubxonada dars tayyorlayotgan talabalarga xalaqit bermang.
Biz yashagan mahalla juda tinch edi.

mistakes.wrong: Odam kim kecha keldi mening akam.
mistakes.note: Uzbek does not use relative pronouns like 'kim' (who) or 'qaysi' (which); place the participle '-gan' directly before the head noun.

mistakes.wrong: Men oʻqiydigan kitobni kecha sotib oldim.
mistakes.right: Men oʻqiyotgan (or oʻqigan) kitobni kecha sotib oldim.
mistakes.note: Use -gan for completed actions or -yotgan for current progress, reserving -(a)digan for habitual or impending future actions.
Avoid appending redundant predicate copulas when forming standard past descriptive clauses.

quiz.question: Kecha majlisda nutq soʻzla___ vakil Samarqanddan keldi.
quiz.explanation: The action occurred yesterday ('kecha'), calling for the past/completed participle -gan.

quiz.question: Har kuni bu koʻchadan oʻta___ avtobus qatnovi toʻxtatildi.
quiz.explanation: 'Har kuni' indicates regular habitual motion, requiring the habitual participle -(a)digan.

quiz.question: Hozir choy ich___ mehmonlar bilan gaplashamiz.
quiz.explanation: 'Hozir' marks an action currently in progress, demanding the continuous participle -yotgan.

quiz.question: Biz ertaga bor___ qishloq togʻlar orasida joylashgan.
quiz.explanation: An action scheduled for tomorrow ('ertaga') takes the future-oriented participle -adigan.

tip: Think of Uzbek relative clauses as giant adjectives: everything modifying the noun goes BEFORE that noun, ending with -gan or -(a)digan!

title: Verbal Nouns (-ish and -(u)v) in Complex Clauses
subtitle: Turn entire actions into nominal clauses taking noun suffixes
keyPoint: Verbal nouns formed with -ish (or -(u)v) nominalize verb stems so they can accept possessive affixes, plural suffixes, and case endings.

examples.en: Sizning bu yerga kelishingiz bizni xursand qildi.
Yigʻilish boshlanishidan avval hamma joylashib oldi.

mistakes.note: When a nominalized action is the direct object of verbs like 'yaxshi koʻrmoq', use -ish with the accusative suffix -ni, not bare -moq.
Postpositions like 'oldin' require the ablative -dan attached to a verbal noun (-ish + possessive + -dan).
The verbal noun must agree with the subject pronoun in person (siz -> kelishingiz).

quiz.question: Darsga kechik___ sababini tushuntirib bering.
quiz.explanation: The verbal noun takes the genitive suffix -ning to connect with 'sababi' ('the reason of being late').

quiz.question: Sport bilan muntazam shugʻullanish salomatlik uchun ___ .
quiz.explanation: 'Shugʻullanish' acts as the syntactic subject described by the predicate adjective 'muhim' (important).

quiz.question: Sizning oʻz vaqtida kel___ barcha masalani hal qildi.
quiz.explanation: 'Sizning' (2nd person formal genitive) requires the verbal noun with matching possessive suffix '-ishingiz'.

quiz.question: Mehmonlar kelishidan ___ xonani tozalab qoʻydik.
quiz.explanation: The ablative nominal phrase 'kelishidan' pairs with the postposition 'oldin' to mean 'before the guests arrived'.

tip: Whenever you want to use 'before doing' or 'after doing' in Uzbek, build the phrase: Stem + -ish + Possessive + -dan oldin/keyin!

title: Conditional Mood (-sa) and Hypotheticals
subtitle: Express 'if', 'when', and hypothetical 'would' using the versatile suffix -sa
keyPoint: Attach the suffix -sa directly to the verb stem followed by personal endings to form real conditions, temporal triggers, or unreal counterfactuals with edi.

cells: if only I had gone / had I gone

useCases.label: Real Condition
useCases.example: Ertaga yomgʻir yogʻsa, biz uyda qolamiz.

useCases.label: Unreal / Counterfactual Wish
useCases.example: Vaqtim koʻp boʻlsa edi, sizga yordam berardim.

examples.en: Ertaga havo yaxshi boʻlsa, toqqa chiqamiz.
Pulim yetarli boʻlsa edi, yangi mashina sotib olardim.
Uyga yetib borsangiz, menga qoʻngʻiroq qiling.
Ular taklif etsa ham, bu majlisga bormayman.

mistakes.note: The conjunction 'agar' (if) requires the verb to carry the conditional suffix -sa, not simple indicative tense.
Conditional verbs must agree in person with the subject (sen borsang, not borsa).
Counterfactual conditionals with -sa edi require an unreal past or habitual past (-ar edi) in the main result clause.

quiz.question: If you study hard, you ___ the exam successfully.
quiz.explanation: The 'if' clause already contains the condition; the main clause requires the declarative future/present tense (topshirasiz).

quiz.question: Vaqtingiz boʻsh ___, birga kofe ichaylik.
quiz.explanation: -sa marks the conditional clause ('If your time is free').

quiz.question: Agar u rost gapirganida yoki aytganida ___ edi, hamma tushunardi.
quiz.explanation: 'boʻlsa edi' completes the counterfactual construction meaning 'if it had been'.

quiz.question: Menga xat ___ , darhol javob qaytaraman.
quiz.explanation: The second person formal conditional suffix is -sangiz ('if you write').

tip: Even though 'agar' means 'if', native Uzbek speakers frequently drop 'agar' altogether because -sa on the verb already carries the complete conditional meaning.

title: Indirective / Evidential Past (-ibdi)
subtitle: Express hearsay, secondhand reports, and unexpected sudden discoveries
keyPoint: Use -ibdi (or -pti after voiceless consonants) when reporting an action you did not witness firsthand or one you just discovered with surprise.

mistakes.wrong: Men kecha kinoga bordim-ku, ammo bilmabman.
mistakes.note: Do not use -ibdi for deliberate actions you witnessed and performed knowingly yourself; use direct past -di.
When repeating reported information that you heard from others, -ibdi is far more natural than the direct witness marker -di.
When inferring a state after the fact, use the evidential -ibdi or ekan rather than simple indicative statements.

quiz.question: Oh no! I have mistakenly left my keys at the office! (Sudden realization)
quiz.explanation: The 1st person mirative suffix -ibman expresses sudden discovery of something you did unconsciously.

quiz.question: According to the news, the president ___ to Samarkand yesterday.
quiz.explanation: Hearsay and reported information without personal witnessing takes the evidential -ibdi.

quiz.question: Tashqariga qara, hamma joy oqarib ketibdi, demak qor ___.
quiz.explanation: Drawing a logical inference from observable evidence requires evidential -ibdi.

quiz.question: Singlim menga aytdi: akam yangi ishga ___.
quiz.explanation: Indirect reported news about a third person takes 3rd person evidential -ibdi.

tip: Think of -ibdi as the 'eureka' or 'rumor' tense: use it whenever your brain processes resultative evidence rather than witnessing the event live.

title: Causative, Passive, and Reflexive Voice Derivation
subtitle: Alter verb transitivity using -dir, -t, -ir, and passive -(i)l
keyPoint: Uzbek changes grammatical voice systematically by inserting derivational affixes directly between the verb root and the tense/mood markers.

examples.en: Bu yangilik butun shaharga tezda tarqaldi.

mistakes.note: If you caused the friend to write it rather than writing it yourself, you must use the causative affix -dir-.
An inanimate patient receiving the action requires the passive voice (-l / -il).
'Tuzalmoq' is intransitive ('to get cured/better'); to actively fix an object, use the transitive causative form 'tuzatmoq'.

quiz.question: The university library was opened last week. Kutubxona oʻtgan haftada ___.
quiz.explanation: The passive form of och- (open) is ochil- (to be opened).

quiz.question: The teacher made the students memorize the poem. Oʻqituvchi oʻquvchilarga sheʼrni ___.
quiz.explanation: Stems ending in a vowel like yodla- take the causative suffix -t, forming yodlat- ('to make memorize').

quiz.question: Qurilish ishlari nihoyasiga ___.
quiz.explanation: Compound passive causative: yet-kaz-il-di means 'was brought to completion'.

quiz.question: Shifokor bemorni dori ichishga majbur qildi va dorini ___.
quiz.explanation: The root ich- (drink) takes the causative -ir- to mean 'cause to drink / administer'.

tip: Remember: if a verb root ends in a liquid sound like 'l' (e.g., bil-), it takes -in instead of -il to form the passive (bilinmoq), avoiding an awkward double 'l'.

title: The Defective Verb E- (Ekan, Emish, Eydi)
subtitle: Encode epistemic doubt, reported gossip, and surprise using ekan and emish
keyPoint: The defective root e- cannot stand alone as a bare verb, but its forms ekan (realization/inference) and emish (allegation/hearsay) serve as essential modal qualifiers.

examples.en: U oʻzini eng aqlli deb hisoblar emish.

mistakes.wrong: U kecha kelgan emish, men koʻrdim.
mistakes.right: U kecha kelgan ekan / keldi, men koʻrdim.
mistakes.note: Do not use 'emish' if you personally observed and vouch for the fact; 'emish' explicitly questions or disclaims credibility.

mistakes.wrong: Bu ovqat mazali edi! (when tasting it right now)
mistakes.note: When tasting food and realizing right now that it is delicious, use 'ekan' to express current discovery, not past 'edi'.
The negative copula 'emas' must precede the hearsay modal 'emish'.

quiz.question: I just tasted this tea: 'Turns out this tea is very sweet!'
quiz.explanation: 'ekan' indicates spontaneous firsthand discovery in the present moment.

quiz.question: Supposedly (rumor has it), he got promoted to director.
quiz.explanation: 'emish' marks hearsay, rumors, or unverified second-hand claims.

quiz.question: U oʻz ishini juda yaxshi biladi deb oʻylagandim, ammo hech narsa bilmas ___.
quiz.explanation: 'bilmas ekan' marks the unexpected revelation that the person in fact knew nothing.

quiz.question: Gʻiybatchilarning aytishicha, u qimmatbaho mashina yutib olgan ___.
quiz.explanation: Gossip ('Gʻiybatchilar') strongly pairs with the skeptical hearsay clitic 'emish'.

tip: A quick rule of thumb: 'Ekan' means 'Aha! I see it is so!', while 'Emish' means 'So they claim, but who knows?'

title: Specialized Temporal and Purposive Converbs
subtitle: Connect complex events with -gach, -guncha, and -gani
keyPoint: Uzbek uses specialized non-finite verbal converbs like -gach (upon doing), -guncha (until), and -gani (in order to) to link subordinate actions seamlessly without conjunctions.

cells: upon arriving / as soon as he came

useCases.label: Upon Completion (-gach)
useCases.example: Uyga kelgach, darhol dars qilishga oʻtirdi.

examples.en: Biz yangi filmni tomosha qilgani kinoteatrga keldik.

mistakes.wrong: Men kitobni oʻqish uchun bordim (to the library).
mistakes.note: With verbs of motion like 'bormoq' or 'kelmoq', the converb -gani is far more natural than using the postposition 'uchun'.
-gach already contains the temporal relation 'upon/after'; combining it with 'paytda' is redundant.
The suffix -guncha already expresses 'until'; adding 'qadar' is redundant in standard Uzbek.

quiz.question: We worked non-stop until the sun went down. Quyosh ___ tinimsiz ishladik.
quiz.explanation: -guncha expresses 'until' a temporal boundary is met.

quiz.question: Immediately upon arriving in Tashkent, he phoned his parents.
quiz.explanation: -gach signifies 'upon / immediately after doing'.

quiz.question: Onam meva sotib ___ bozorga ketdi.
quiz.explanation: Motion towards a destination with an objective requires the purposive converb -gani ('in order to buy').

quiz.question: U darsga ___ uchun mavzuni yaxshi tushunmadi.
quiz.explanation: -gani uchun expresses reason/cause ('because he did not come').

tip: Pay attention to consonant harmony: the initial 'g' in -gach, -guncha, and -gani hardens to 'k' after voiceless consonants (ek-kach) and to 'q' after back velar 'q' (chiq-qach).
